newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to pull out embassy staff from Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to pull out embassy staff from Cambodia.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday it was pulling about 40 diplomats and their dependents out of Cambodia but would keep the mission open.
Washington also told Hun Sen, whose forces control Phnom Penh after days of fighting, that the international community would not tolerate the killing of political opponents.

"We are very concerned and obviously disturbed by the fact that the democracy that is beginning to grow in Cambodia, that the people of Cambodia voted for in overwhelming numbers two years ago, is now subjected to this kind of force," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said in an interview with public television.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the U.S. diplomats were leaving because of the "uncertain security situation" after days of fighting across the country.

"We currently have 61 official American diplomats in Cambodia. We will draw them down to a total of 20 American diplomats in the next couple of days and we'll hold there," he told a regular State Department news conference.
He also said that between 1,000 and 1,300 other Americans in Phnom Penh and elsewhere in the Southeast Asian state were being urged to leave over the next few days.

He said although the Pentagon had made contingency plans for a possible military evacuation, it was hoped the diplomats and others could leave by civilian transport now that flights were being restored at Phnom Penh airport.
The U.S. embassy in Bangkok was preparing to help those coming out.
"Fortunately, the situation in Phnom Penh is quieter than it has been at any time over the last four or five days," Burns added, although he said there was still sporadic shooting in the capital.

Fierce fighting erupted over the weekend as forces of Hun Sen battled those of his co-prime minister Prince Ranariddh. Burns said of Hun Sen: "He bears enormous responsibility for having ignited this fire."

He said the Cambodian ambassador was being called to the U.S. State Department on Wednesday afternoon to be told of Washington's "very serious concerns" about reports of political killings that followed the fighting.

"We are aware of reports of political assassinations and political killings, including reports that an associate of Prince Ranariddh, Ho Sok, was killed yesterday while he was in the custody of the political party of Hun Sen.
"The United States condemns this killing. We're very disturbed by reports that indicate that responsibility for this killing lies with Hun Sen and his associates," he said.
Hun Sen had been told through the U.S. ambassador in Phnom Penh that "this type of activity will not be tolerated or supported in any way by the international community," he said.

Burns said Ranariddh was on his way to the United States from France for meetings with United Nations officials in New York and would probably meet on Friday with Acting Secretary of State Thomas Pickering, who is standing in while Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is in Europe.
He said Washington had "given some advice" to the members of ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) meeting to discuss Cambodia on Thursday.

He refused to say specifically what that advice was but said: "It's very important at a time like this when there's chaos in Cambodia, when they're on the verge of a Civil War, when fighting is occurring throughout the country between forces of the two major political parties, for countries that have an interest in Cambodia to speak out about what is acceptable and what is not acceptable."

Asked in an interview with public television's "NewsHour with Jim Lehrer" if the United States favoured one side in the Cambodian struggle, Albright said, "No, we don't have a favourite, but we do not believe that Hun Sen having taken over by force is an appropriate way to deal with governmental change."
